REASONS FOR DECISION

[1] XXXX XXXX XXXX (the claimant), is claiming refugee protection pursuant to section 96 and subsection 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act.1
ALLEGATIONS

[3] The claimant alleges that he came to the United States in March 1993 and made an unsuccessful claim for refugee protection in 1998. His claim was based on his violation of the family planning policy. His appeal was denied in September 2003. Due to administrative issues dealing with documentation of the decision, it was necessary to re-issue the appeal decision of 2003 in March 2007. As a result of his unsuccessful claim for refugee protection and unsuccessful appeal, the claimant was ordered to leave the United States however he remained in the United States.

[4] The claimant was detained in North Carolina from XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX until XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. Upon his release from detention he continued to remain in the United States.

[5] In 2009, the claimant alleges that he joined the China Democracy Party. As a member, he alleges that he attended meetings and promoted the party's policies.

[6] In November 2010, the claimant began to practice Falun Gong which he believed would help resolve pain in his shoulder.

[7] The claimant alleges that in May 2011, many people without status in the United States were being sent back to their home countries.

[8] The claimant left the United States and entered Canada from Seattle, Washington on XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX He claimant made his application for refugee protection in Canada on July 21, 2011.
DETERMINATION

[9] For the reasons that follow, the panel finds that the claimant would not face a serious possibility of persecution on a Convention ground and, on a balance of probabilities, would not personally be subjected to a risk to life or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment or a danger of torture upon his return to the People's Republic of China.

[10] Therefore the panel finds that the claimant is not a Convention refugee and does not have a well-founded fear of persecution or harm should he return to the People's Republic of China.
ANALYSIS

[11] In assessing this claim, the panel focused on the credibility of the claimant's allegations of the risk of persecution or harm he might face upon his return to the People's Republic of China.

[12] The panel is cognizant of the difficulties faced by the claimant in establishing his claim. These include cultural factors, the environment of the hearing room, his limited formal education and the stress inherent in responding to oral questions through an interpreter. The panel has taken these considerations into account in arriving at its determination.

[15] A determinative issue in this claim is the claimant's personal and national identity. On a balance of probabilities, for the following reasons, the panel finds that claimant has not provided adequate documentation in support of his personal identity and national identity as a citizen of the People's Republic of China. Further, the panel finds that the claimant has not made sufficient efforts to obtain such documents.

[16] In the analysis of the claimant's identity, the panel is guided by section 106 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act which states:
The Refugee Protection Division must take into account, with respect to the credibility of a claimant, whether the claimant possesses acceptable documentation establishing identity, and if not, whether they have provided a reasonable explanation for the lack of documentation or have taken reasonable steps to obtain the documentation.3

[17] Furthermore, the panel is guided by Rule11 of the Refugee Protection Division Rules that states:

[18] The claimant must provide acceptable documents establishing identity and other elements of the claim. A claimant who does not provide acceptable documents must explain why they were not provided and what steps were taken to obtain them.4

[19] The Federal Court has held that, "The claimant has the fundamental obligation to establish his or her identity, on a balance of probabilities."5 Additionally, "The claimant must come to a hearing with all of the evidence that he or she is able to offer and believes is necessary to prove a claim."6 Madame Justice Snider stated, "[p]roof of identity is a prerequisite for a person claiming refugee protection, as without it there can 'be no sound basis for testing or verifying the claims of persecution or indeed for determining the Applicant's true nationality.'"7

[20] In this matter, the claimant indicated in his initial Claim for Refugee Protection Form dated July 19, 2011,8 that he traveled to the United States on a false passport and according to his Personal Information Form he entered Canada without any documents.9 If the claimant did travel on false documents, or had no documents, it would be reasonable to expect that he make every effort to establish his identity. The claimant has an experienced counsel who understands the importance of establishing one's identity for a refugee claim.

[21] In light of the foregoing, it is reasonable to expect that the claimant would have made some serious efforts to obtain documents to verify his identity and nationality. For the following reasons, the panel finds that the photocopies and original documents the claimant produced have little probative value.

[22] The claimant provided a, civil mediation certificate,10 photocopies of household registration,11 marriage certificate,12 membership card of the China Democracy Party, Illinois identification card,13 employment authorization card,14 United States social security card15 and notarial certificate.16 The panel finds that none of these documents contain security features such as those found in the Resident Identity Card or a passport. After considering the claimant's testimony and his explanations, the panel finds that he has not established his personal and national identity, on a balance of probabilities.
Resident Identity Card

[23] The claimant did not submit into evidence an original or copy of his Resident Identity Card. This is a critical document that established both personal and national identity.

[24] Initially implemented by the Chinese Government in 1985, The Resident Identity Card is the most important document to establish the claimant's identity as a national of the People's Republic of China. (RIC). Every Chinese citizen over the age of 16 must have one.17 The claimant testified that he had given the card to the smuggler who was going to return it when his fee was paid by his wife. The claimant testified that the fee was paid but the card was not returned to his wife. When asked what efforts he made to get the card back, the claimant testified that his wife, "did not even ask to get it back, it did not occur to her that I needed it." When asked if he had followed up, the claimant replied that he did not as it was difficult to find the smuggler. The panel finds it is reasonable to expect that the claimant would have made some serious efforts to obtain this important document to verify his identity and nationality.
Passport

[25] The claimant did not provide a passport issued by the People's Republic of China. When asked by the panel if he had one and where it was, the claimant testified that he did not. The panel finds it reasonable to expect that for the claimant to travel around the United States by plane, he would have to provide proper identification documents such as a passport or official government identification.
Availability of Fraudulent Documents in China

[26] For the following reasons the panel finds that the claimant was aware of the availability of fraudulent documents. In his Declaration found on page 10 of his Claim for Refugee Protection, the claimant signed a declaration indicating that the contents of that document were truthful, complete and correct.18

subthemes.text:
[27] He claims in his July 19, 2011 Claim for Refugee Protection in response to question 22 that the agent "provided a false passport."19 In correspondence with the Research Directorate, an official at the Canadian Embassy in Beijing wrote that, "There are 'consistent reports' of document fraud in China and that fraudulent identity documents (IDs) are easily obtained in the country."20

[28] Similarly, a professor of criminal justice at Xavier University who specializes in Chinese policing stated in correspondence with the Research Directorate that, "[t]here is little question that fraud of all kind[s], including ID fraud, is a major problem in China."21 The professor added that:
Fraudulent IDs are "easily accessible" and that the industry is a "big business" and an "open secret" in China. In July 2012, the state media source China.org.cn described the fraudulent ID industry as "an incredibly lucrative trade," in an article about the market for fake student ID cards, university diplomas, and other types of ID on the grounds of Renmin University in Beijing. According to the Beijing embassy official, the provinces of Guangdong and Fujian are "considered particularly high-risk for fraudulent documents."22
Hukou

[29] The claimant tendered into evidence a photocopy of his family Hukou. The claimant testified that the judge in the United States did not return the Hukou and his lawyer in the United States may not have returned the original. The claimant indicated that he tried to contact the lawyer but was unable to do so as they had moved. Regardless of the absence of the original document, for the following reasons, the panel finds that this document does not establish the national identity of the claimant. The Hukou does not contain the security features that are found in the government issued Resident Identity Card and the passport issued by the government of the People's Republic of China.

[30] Furthermore, the household register (Hukou) appears to be extremely susceptible to fraud and manipulation.23 A United States (US) consular official stationed in southern China states that, "You can't trust any [personal] documents in China."24 The official also stated that the market for fraudulent documents is rapidly expanding and that documents, "Are presumed to be fraudulent unless proven otherwise." In 2009, a professor of international affairs at Georgina Institute of Technology, who has published on the Hukou system in China, stated that both Hukou forgery and acquiring genuine Hukou by fraudulent means has been occurring in China for many years. Furthermore, in reviewing the Hukou provided by the claimant, the panel notes that country documentary evidence indicates that there exists a proliferation of fraudulent Chinese documents.25 The panel has considered the country documents, which state "Fake Hukou booklets are common and that they can be purchased easily on the black market and even semi-open market." As such the panel can give the Hukou little weight in corroborating the claimant's residency in China at the material time.
Credibility

subthemes.text:
[33] When a claimant swears that certain facts are true, this creates a presumption that they are indeed true unless there is valid reason to doubt their veracity.27 The determination as to whether a claimant's evidence is credible is made, on a balance of probabilities.28

[34] The panel has concerns regarding the credibility of some aspects of the claimant's evidence. At the outset of the hearing the claimant affirmed that his Personal Information Form was true, accurate and complete. Further, he signed a declaration to that effect. In testimony, the claimant indicated that he entered the United States through Mexico. When asked why he did not include this information in his narrative, the claimant testified that he told his lawyer but the information regarding his entry into the United States was omitted. The panel pointed out that it was his responsibility to ensure the accuracy of his Personal Information Form. The claimant testified that he had little formal education and therefore did not understand many aspects of the application process. The panel notes that the claimant was represented by competent counsel. As well, even with his limited formal education, the panel notes that the claimant was able to arrange his departure from the People's Republic of China, his arrival in the United States where he remained from 1993 to 2011, his applications and appeals for refugee protection in the United States, his departure from the United States ad his arrival and application for refugee protection in Canada.

[35] The panel has chosen to rely on the documentary evidence of the the People's Republic of China 29 National Documentation Package (NDP) as this information because it originates from a variety of reputable independent sources, which would reasonably, is expected to be knowledgeable with respect to the situation in the People's Republic of China. The documentary evidence is seen as reliable, probative, detailed information, so as to provide the panel with a thorough understanding of the situation of the People's Republic of China.

[36] In situations where a claimant has not established his identity, a negative conclusion as to credibility will almost inevitably be drawn, and can, in and of itself, be dispositive of the claim.30 In addition, the Federal Court held that once the panel concluded that the identity of the claimant has not been established, it was not necessary to analyze the evidence any further.31 Based on the foregoing analysis, the panel finds that this is the situation in this case.

[37] On the basis of the totality of the evidence and the cumulative findings noted above, the panel finds that the claimant has not satisfied his burden of establishing his personal and national identity and therefore, his claim for refugee protection has not been established.
CONCLUSION

[33] When a claimant swears that certain facts are true, this creates a presumption that they are indeed true unless there is valid reason to doubt their veracity.27 The determination as to whether a claimant's evidence is credible is made, on a balance of probabilities.28

[34] The panel has concerns regarding the credibility of some aspects of the claimant's evidence. At the outset of the hearing the claimant affirmed that his Personal Information Form was true, accurate and complete. Further, he signed a declaration to that effect. In testimony, the claimant indicated that he entered the United States through Mexico. When asked why he did not include this information in his narrative, the claimant testified that he told his lawyer but the information regarding his entry into the United States was omitted. The panel pointed out that it was his responsibility to ensure the accuracy of his Personal Information Form. The claimant testified that he had little formal education and therefore did not understand many aspects of the application process. The panel notes that the claimant was represented by competent counsel. As well, even with his limited formal education, the panel notes that the claimant was able to arrange his departure from the People's Republic of China, his arrival in the United States where he remained from 1993 to 2011, his applications and appeals for refugee protection in the United States, his departure from the United States ad his arrival and application for refugee protection in Canada.

[35] The panel has chosen to rely on the documentary evidence of the the People's Republic of China 29 National Documentation Package (NDP) as this information because it originates from a variety of reputable independent sources, which would reasonably, is expected to be knowledgeable with respect to the situation in the People's Republic of China. The documentary evidence is seen as reliable, probative, detailed information, so as to provide the panel with a thorough understanding of the situation of the People's Republic of China.

[36] In situations where a claimant has not established his identity, a negative conclusion as to credibility will almost inevitably be drawn, and can, in and of itself, be dispositive of the claim.30 In addition, the Federal Court held that once the panel concluded that the identity of the claimant has not been established, it was not necessary to analyze the evidence any further.31 Based on the foregoing analysis, the panel finds that this is the situation in this case.

[37] On the basis of the totality of the evidence and the cumulative findings noted above, the panel finds that the claimant has not satisfied his burden of establishing his personal and national identity and therefore, his claim for refugee protection has not been established.
CONCLUSION

Reasons and Decision ? Motifs et Décision
Claimant(s)
XXXX XXXX
Demandeur(e)(s) d'asile
Date(s) of Hearing
May 28, 2018
Date(s) de l'audience

Conseil(s) du (de la/des) demandeur(e)(s) d'asile

REASONS FOR DECISION

[1] XXXX XXXX XXXX (the claimant), is claiming refugee protection pursuant to section 96 and subsection 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act.1
ALLEGATIONS

[2] The complete story alleging the basis of the claimant's fear is captured in the claimant's Personal Information Form (PIF).2 The following is a summary of the narrative and the timeline based on the panel's understanding of the documents disclosed by the claimant.

[3] The claimant alleges that he came to the United States in March 1993 and made an unsuccessful claim for refugee protection in 1998. His claim was based on his violation of the family planning policy. His appeal was denied in September 2003. Due to administrative issues dealing with documentation of the decision, it was necessary to re-issue the appeal decision of 2003 in March 2007. As a result of his unsuccessful claim for refugee protection and unsuccessful appeal, the claimant was ordered to leave the United States however he remained in the United States.
[4] The claimant was detained in North Carolina from XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX until XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. Upon his release from detention he continued to remain in the United States.
[5] In 2009, the claimant alleges that he joined the China Democracy Party. As a member, he alleges that he attended meetings and promoted the party's policies.
[6] In November 2010, the claimant began to practice Falun Gong which he believed would help resolve pain in his shoulder.
[7] The claimant alleges that in May 2011, many people without status in the United States were being sent back to their home countries.

[8] The claimant left the United States and entered Canada from Seattle, Washington on XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX He claimant made his application for refugee protection in Canada on July 21, 2011.
DETERMINATION

[9] For the reasons that follow, the panel finds that the claimant would not face a serious possibility of persecution on a Convention ground and, on a balance of probabilities, would not personally be subjected to a risk to life or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment or a danger of torture upon his return to the People's Republic of China.

[10] Therefore the panel finds that the claimant is not a Convention refugee and does not have a well-founded fear of persecution or harm should he return to the People's Republic of China.
ANALYSIS
[11] In assessing this claim, the panel focused on the credibility of the claimant's allegations of the risk of persecution or harm he might face upon his return to the People's Republic of China.

[12] The panel is cognizant of the difficulties faced by the claimant in establishing his claim. These include cultural factors, the environment of the hearing room, his limited formal education and the stress inherent in responding to oral questions through an interpreter. The panel has taken these considerations into account in arriving at its determination.

[13] The panel identified the following issues in this claim; the claimant's personal and national identity, the credibility of the claimant's allegation concerning his violation of the family planning policy, his practice of Falun Gong and his pursuit by authorities in China because of that practice, and, the potential sur place nature of his claim. The panel finds, on a balance of probabilities, that the claimant has not been a credible witness in regard. The reasons for these findings are noted below.

[14] At the outset of the hearing, the claimant was asked by the panel if there were any additional documents that he wanted to provide but could not. He replied that the panel had all the documents he wished to provide.
IDENTITY

[15] A determinative issue in this claim is the claimant's personal and national identity. On a balance of probabilities, for the following reasons, the panel finds that claimant has not provided adequate documentation in support of his personal identity and national identity as a citizen of the People's Republic of China. Further, the panel finds that the claimant has not made sufficient efforts to obtain such documents.

[16] In the analysis of the claimant's identity, the panel is guided by section 106 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act which states:
The Refugee Protection Division must take into account, with respect to the credibility of a claimant, whether the claimant possesses acceptable documentation establishing identity, and if not, whether they have provided a reasonable explanation for the lack of documentation or have taken reasonable steps to obtain the documentation.3
[17] Furthermore, the panel is guided by Rule11 of the Refugee Protection Division Rules that states:

[18] The claimant must provide acceptable documents establishing identity and other elements of the claim. A claimant who does not provide acceptable documents must explain why they were not provided and what steps were taken to obtain them.4

[19] The Federal Court has held that, "The claimant has the fundamental obligation to establish his or her identity, on a balance of probabilities."5 Additionally, "The claimant must come to a hearing with all of the evidence that he or she is able to offer and believes is necessary to prove a claim."6 Madame Justice Snider stated, "[p]roof of identity is a prerequisite for a person claiming refugee protection, as without it there can 'be no sound basis for testing or verifying the claims of persecution or indeed for determining the Applicant's true nationality.'"7

[20] In this matter, the claimant indicated in his initial Claim for Refugee Protection Form dated July 19, 2011,8 that he traveled to the United States on a false passport and according to his Personal Information Form he entered Canada without any documents.9 If the claimant did travel on false documents, or had no documents, it would be reasonable to expect that he make every effort to establish his identity. The claimant has an experienced counsel who understands the importance of establishing one's identity for a refugee claim.

[21] In light of the foregoing, it is reasonable to expect that the claimant would have made some serious efforts to obtain documents to verify his identity and nationality. For the following reasons, the panel finds that the photocopies and original documents the claimant produced have little probative value.

[22] The claimant provided a, civil mediation certificate,10 photocopies of household registration,11 marriage certificate,12 membership card of the China Democracy Party, Illinois identification card,13 employment authorization card,14 United States social security card15 and notarial certificate.16 The panel finds that none of these documents contain security features such as those found in the Resident Identity Card or a passport. After considering the claimant's testimony and his explanations, the panel finds that he has not established his personal and national identity, on a balance of probabilities.
Resident Identity Card
[23] The claimant did not submit into evidence an original or copy of his Resident Identity Card. This is a critical document that established both personal and national identity.

[24] Initially implemented by the Chinese Government in 1985, The Resident Identity Card is the most important document to establish the claimant's identity as a national of the People's Republic of China. (RIC). Every Chinese citizen over the age of 16 must have one.17 The claimant testified that he had given the card to the smuggler who was going to return it when his fee was paid by his wife. The claimant testified that the fee was paid but the card was not returned to his wife. When asked what efforts he made to get the card back, the claimant testified that his wife, "did not even ask to get it back, it did not occur to her that I needed it." When asked if he had followed up, the claimant replied that he did not as it was difficult to find the smuggler. The panel finds it is reasonable to expect that the claimant would have made some serious efforts to obtain this important document to verify his identity and nationality.
Passport

[25] The claimant did not provide a passport issued by the People's Republic of China. When asked by the panel if he had one and where it was, the claimant testified that he did not. The panel finds it reasonable to expect that for the claimant to travel around the United States by plane, he would have to provide proper identification documents such as a passport or official government identification.
Availability of Fraudulent Documents in China

[26] For the following reasons the panel finds that the claimant was aware of the availability of fraudulent documents. In his Declaration found on page 10 of his Claim for Refugee Protection, the claimant signed a declaration indicating that the contents of that document were truthful, complete and correct.18

[27] He claims in his July 19, 2011 Claim for Refugee Protection in response to question 22 that the agent "provided a false passport."19 In correspondence with the Research Directorate, an official at the Canadian Embassy in Beijing wrote that, "There are 'consistent reports' of document fraud in China and that fraudulent identity documents (IDs) are easily obtained in the country."20

[28] Similarly, a professor of criminal justice at Xavier University who specializes in Chinese policing stated in correspondence with the Research Directorate that, "[t]here is little question that fraud of all kind[s], including ID fraud, is a major problem in China."21 The professor added that:
Fraudulent IDs are "easily accessible" and that the industry is a "big business" and an "open secret" in China. In July 2012, the state media source China.org.cn described the fraudulent ID industry as "an incredibly lucrative trade," in an article about the market for fake student ID cards, university diplomas, and other types of ID on the grounds of Renmin University in Beijing. According to the Beijing embassy official, the provinces of Guangdong and Fujian are "considered particularly high-risk for fraudulent documents."22
Hukou

[29] The claimant tendered into evidence a photocopy of his family Hukou. The claimant testified that the judge in the United States did not return the Hukou and his lawyer in the United States may not have returned the original. The claimant indicated that he tried to contact the lawyer but was unable to do so as they had moved. Regardless of the absence of the original document, for the following reasons, the panel finds that this document does not establish the national identity of the claimant. The Hukou does not contain the security features that are found in the government issued Resident Identity Card and the passport issued by the government of the People's Republic of China.

[30] Furthermore, the household register (Hukou) appears to be extremely susceptible to fraud and manipulation.23 A United States (US) consular official stationed in southern China states that, "You can't trust any [personal] documents in China."24 The official also stated that the market for fraudulent documents is rapidly expanding and that documents, "Are presumed to be fraudulent unless proven otherwise." In 2009, a professor of international affairs at Georgina Institute of Technology, who has published on the Hukou system in China, stated that both Hukou forgery and acquiring genuine Hukou by fraudulent means has been occurring in China for many years. Furthermore, in reviewing the Hukou provided by the claimant, the panel notes that country documentary evidence indicates that there exists a proliferation of fraudulent Chinese documents.25 The panel has considered the country documents, which state "Fake Hukou booklets are common and that they can be purchased easily on the black market and even semi-open market." As such the panel can give the Hukou little weight in corroborating the claimant's residency in China at the material time.
Credibility
[31] For the following reasons, the panel identified some concerns in regard to the claimant's overall credibility.

[32] In situations where a claimant has not established his identity, a negative conclusion as to credibility will almost inevitably be drawn, and can, in and of itself, be dispositive of the claim.26

[33] When a claimant swears that certain facts are true, this creates a presumption that they are indeed true unless there is valid reason to doubt their veracity.27 The determination as to whether a claimant's evidence is credible is made, on a balance of probabilities.28

[34] The panel has concerns regarding the credibility of some aspects of the claimant's evidence. At the outset of the hearing the claimant affirmed that his Personal Information Form was true, accurate and complete. Further, he signed a declaration to that effect. In testimony, the claimant indicated that he entered the United States through Mexico. When asked why he did not include this information in his narrative, the claimant testified that he told his lawyer but the information regarding his entry into the United States was omitted. The panel pointed out that it was his responsibility to ensure the accuracy of his Personal Information Form. The claimant testified that he had little formal education and therefore did not understand many aspects of the application process. The panel notes that the claimant was represented by competent counsel. As well, even with his limited formal education, the panel notes that the claimant was able to arrange his departure from the People's Republic of China, his arrival in the United States where he remained from 1993 to 2011, his applications and appeals for refugee protection in the United States, his departure from the United States ad his arrival and application for refugee protection in Canada.

[35] The panel has chosen to rely on the documentary evidence of the the People's Republic of China 29 National Documentation Package (NDP) as this information because it originates from a variety of reputable independent sources, which would reasonably, is expected to be knowledgeable with respect to the situation in the People's Republic of China. The documentary evidence is seen as reliable, probative, detailed information, so as to provide the panel with a thorough understanding of the situation of the People's Republic of China.

[36] In situations where a claimant has not established his identity, a negative conclusion as to credibility will almost inevitably be drawn, and can, in and of itself, be dispositive of the claim.30 In addition, the Federal Court held that once the panel concluded that the identity of the claimant has not been established, it was not necessary to analyze the evidence any further.31 Based on the foregoing analysis, the panel finds that this is the situation in this case.

[37] On the basis of the totality of the evidence and the cumulative findings noted above, the panel finds that the claimant has not satisfied his burden of establishing his personal and national identity and therefore, his claim for refugee protection has not been established.
CONCLUSION

[38] The panel therefore finds that the claimant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection. The Refugee Protection Division rejects his claim.
(signed)
